title: Painful facial rash in a man with eczema — recognise danger, assess and act safely

blocks.text: Painful facial rash in a man with eczema — recognise danger, assess and act safely

AMaC MRCP PACES23 · Round 5 · R5-214 · Station 2 acute consultation · 20 minutes · Assessed skills: A clinical assessment, B physical signs where appropriate, C communication, D differential diagnosis, E clinical judgement, F patient concerns, G welfare · Not an official PACES mark scheme.

A 29-year-old with longstanding atopic eczema reports a sudden painful blistering facial eruption, fever and lesions near the eyelid. Assess and explain your management. You are the medical registrar in the acute assessment unit (or appropriately designated acute clinician). Explore concerns, assess risk and explain the immediate plan.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: Hook: Suspected eczema herpeticum (disseminated cutaneous HSV on eczema); distinguish bacterial impetigo and other viral eruptions without withholding antiviral treatment. Examiner trap: Potential herpetic keratitis and vision loss: do not use topical steroid eye drops without ophthalmological advice, and do not delay antivirals for swab results.

blocks.text: Patient is anxious but cooperative. Open with: “I am worried something serious is happening.” Answer history questions using these facts only: Rapid painful monomorphic vesicles or punched-out erosions on eczema, sometimes with fever or malaise; assess periocular skin, red eye, pain, light sensitivity and visual disturbance. Ask “Will I need to stay in hospital?” and accept calm, specific explanations. No unscripted extra examination findings.

Q1. What is the urgent differential?
Model: Eczema herpeticum is high priority; impetigo and other blistering conditions remain differential diagnoses.

Q2. Why ask about visual symptoms?
Model: Periocular disease risks herpetic eye involvement and sight-threatening complications.

Q3. What treatment cannot wait?
Model: Prompt systemic aciclovir and urgent specialist management; do not wait for confirmatory virology.

Q4. Is topical corticosteroid alone sufficient?
Model: No; topical steroid alone misses the potentially serious HSV infection.

Q5. Who should review this patient?
Model: Same-day dermatology and ophthalmology, with admission assessment for systemic illness.
